chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
title: The dark club, the first set and an instant raise
summary: The club was too dark to read music; Holmes played two choruses on 'Sunny Side of the Street' and Kirby raised his pay from $140.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x:
It was getting close to time to hit, you know, in the place. So we all got out there. We got in a cab and went to the club. And boy, it was a little place. It wasn't a big place. A small club. And very dark in there. And on the bandstand, boy, they didn't have no music racks. They had to put the books on the floor. And you couldn't see; you couldn't see the floor, it was so dark in there. And I'm looking, I said, "Man, if this was on a rack I wouldn't be able to see it." So Kirby must have felt, you know, that it wouldn't be too good to be trying to read any music, because you could see that. And he had three new men in the band, too.

So anyway, Kirby started off, he called "Sunny Side Of The Street." So we opened up with "Sunny Side Of The Street," and he told me to take a chorus. Well, I played my chorus, boy, and he hollered. Oh, he screamed! He was so tickled. "Play another one, Charlie. Play another one." So I played another chorus. Boy, he was grinning from ear to ear, and the people were applauding. I said, "All right..." So anyway, Clarence Brewington, he played, and everybody, they got their little applause and one-thing-or-another, you know.

So when we finished the first set, Kirby was so tickled, boy, he come and grabbed me around the shoulder... Because you know, Procope was his man. Nobody could do no wrong as long as Procope was there. And he was so tickled with me, because when Bill Beason had been in the band, he had tried to get me in the band for years, but I never would go with the band. So Kirby, he was tickled to death. He just put his arm around my shoulder, and he said, 'How much did I promise to pay you?' So I told him. Well, he'd promised me a hundred and forty dollars, which I mean, wasn't bad in them days, because I was out in the street gettin' nothin'!
